title: Arguing What Each Would Say
bigQuestion: How do you argue what three traditions would say about a question, using their own texts, without ranking them or flattening them into one?

story.title: Three Texts and One Answer
story.kicker: Maya stands at the front of the room with three quotations, one thesis and nine minutes.
paragraphs: Two weeks after the blank index card, Maya has twenty-six note cards held together with a binder clip. Each one has a citation at the top, an exact quotation, a line about context and a line about how the tradition reads the passage. Her question has not changed: what does each tradition say a person owes to rest, and why? What has changed is that she can now answer it. On the screen behind her, the first slide shows three short passages side by side, each with its source underneath.

The first is from Exodus 20, the Sabbath commandment, in the King James translation. The second is a paraphrase of the Bhagavad Gita, chapter 6, where Krishna tells Arjuna that discipline is not for the person who sleeps too much or too little, but for the one who is moderate in eating, rest, work, sleep and waking. The third is a paraphrase of Analects 1.5, where Confucius says a good ruler employs the people only at the proper seasons. Three kinds of text: a law, a teaching given in a story, and a saying recorded by students.

Maya reads her thesis aloud. Each tradition says a person is owed rest, she argues, but each places that duty somewhere different. The Torah places it in God's command to a whole household, servants and animals included. The Gita places it in the balance of a disciplined self. The Analects place it in the virtue of a ruler who does not wear out the people. A classmate in the second row writes the three places down. That is what a thesis is for: it gives a listener something to hold.

Then come the questions. Does every Jewish family keep the Sabbath the way Exodus describes? Maya says no, and names the differences among Orthodox, Conservative and Reform practice. Isn't the Gita really about a war? Yes, she says, and explains that the teaching on balance is given on a battlefield, and that commentators have read that setting in different ways. Which view do you agree with? She smiles and says the assignment asked what each tradition would say, and that her answer is on the slide. This chapter follows the path from her note cards to that answer.
story.think: Maya declined to say which view she agreed with. Why might a presenter in a public-school course on religion make that choice, and what did she offer instead?

lessons.title: What a Thesis Claims
lessons.mainIdea: A capstone thesis states what each tradition would answer, names the reason each gives, and makes a comparison a reader could test against the texts.
reading: Maya's first draft of a thesis read: Judaism, Hinduism and Confucianism all value rest. Every word of it is true, and it says almost nothing. A *thesis* is the central claim of a paper, the one or two sentences the rest of the paper must prove. A weak thesis lists topics. A strong thesis argues. Her revised version reads: Each tradition says a person is owed rest, but each places that duty in a different spot: the Torah in God's command to the household, the Gita in the balance of a disciplined self, and the Analects in the virtue of a ruler.

The revision works because it has three parts. First, it answers the question for each tradition. Second, it names where each tradition grounds its answer, which is the why. Third, it makes a comparison: the same duty, located in three different places. It is also *arguable*, meaning a careful reader could disagree and would need evidence to settle the matter. Someone might say the Gita cares less about rest than about duty. Maya's paper must show, with the text, why balance is the right word.

Notice the phrase would say. The Torah, the Gita and the Analects were written long before anyone worked twenty hours a week at a grocery store. None of them answers Maya's question directly. So the capstone asks you to reason from what a text does say to what its tradition would likely answer. That reasoning must be visible. Each part of the thesis is a *claim*, and each claim must point to a passage. If the clause about the Gita cannot be tied to a verse, it must be cut or rewritten.

Three thesis mistakes are common. The ranking thesis says one tradition has the healthiest or most advanced view, which no text can prove and which the course does not ask. The sameness thesis says all religions teach the same thing about rest, which erases the differences adherents care about. The lopsided thesis gives one tradition a full answer and the other two a phrase each. The fix for all three is the same: one clear clause per tradition, one grounding per clause, and one sentence that compares them.

words.d: the central claim of a paper, stated in one or two sentences, that the rest of the paper sets out to prove
open to reasonable disagreement, so that evidence is needed to support it
a statement the writer asserts and must support with evidence, such as what a tradition teaches and why

look.title: Balance in the Gita
look.text: Krishna tells Arjuna that the discipline of yoga is not for one who eats too much or fasts too much, nor for one who sleeps too much or stays awake too long. For the person who is moderate in food and recreation, in effort at work, and in sleeping and waking, this discipline takes away sorrow.
look.prompt: Which clause of Maya's thesis does this passage support? Write the one sentence that connects the passage to the clause.

check.q: Why was Maya's first draft, Judaism, Hinduism and Confucianism all value rest, a weak thesis?
choices: It named the traditions but made no argument about why or how they differ
It contained a factual error about Judaism
It ranked the three traditions
It was too long for one sentence
check.why: A weak thesis lists topics. The revision names where each tradition grounds rest and compares them, which is an argument.

check.q: What does the phrase would say ask the student to do?
choices: Report what adherents said in interviews only
Guess freely about a tradition's views
Reason from what a text does say to what its tradition would likely answer, showing the reasoning
Quote a text that answers the modern question word for word
check.why: Ancient texts do not answer modern questions directly, so the student reasons from the passage and makes each step visible.

check.q: Which thesis makes the sameness mistake?
choices: Judaism has the healthiest view of rest
The Torah grounds rest in command, the Gita in balance, and the Analects in a ruler's virtue
The Gita gives the fullest answer, and the other two add a little
All religions teach the same thing about rest
check.why: The sameness thesis erases differences that adherents care about. The first choice ranks, and the third is lopsided.

lessons.title: Evidence in Three Layers
lessons.mainIdea: Strong evidence has three layers, the quoted text, its context and how adherents have read it, joined to the claim by a sentence of reasoning.
reading: In the Torah's law, the Sabbath commandment of Exodus 20 tells a household to stop work on the seventh day. That quotation is the first layer of *evidence*, the text itself. By itself it proves little, because a reader does not yet know what kind of text it is or how anyone has lived by it. A paragraph that drops a quotation and moves on leaves the reader to do the work. The capstone asks you to do that work on the page.

The second layer is *context*: genre, speaker, audience and setting. Exodus 20 is law, presented as given to Israel at Mount Sinai. It names who must rest: children, servants, animals and the foreigner living among the people. Deuteronomy 5 repeats the command and adds a reason, the memory of slavery in Egypt. The third layer is the reading of the community. The Mishnah, the early rabbinic law code compiled about 200 CE, lists thirty-nine categories of forbidden work, called *melakhot*. Rabbinic law also holds that saving a life overrides the Sabbath.

The three layers still need a sentence that joins them to the claim. That sentence is the *warrant*, the reasoning that explains why this evidence supports this claim. Maya writes: Because the commandment lists servants, animals and strangers, and because Deuteronomy ties it to the memory of slavery, the Torah treats rest as something owed to the vulnerable, not only chosen by the free. Without that sentence, a reader sees a verse and a claim sitting side by side, and has to guess how they connect.

Every body paragraph in the capstone can follow the same order. State the claim. Quote the text with its citation. Give the context in a sentence or two. Report how adherents have read it, naming the source. Write the warrant. Five moves, in that order, turn a quotation into an argument. It feels slow at first. By the third tradition it becomes a habit, and a reader can follow every step you took.

words.d: the material that supports a claim; in the capstone, a quoted text together with its context and its reading
the genre, speaker, audience and setting of a passage, which shape what it means
the sentence of reasoning that explains why a piece of evidence supports a claim
in Jewish law, the thirty-nine categories of work that the Mishnah lists as forbidden on the Sabbath

look.title: The Second Reason for the Sabbath
look.text: And remember that thou wast a servant in the land of Egypt, and that the LORD thy God brought thee out thence through a mighty hand and by a stretched out arm: therefore the LORD thy God commanded thee to keep the sabbath day.
look.prompt: Write a warrant that connects this verse to the claim that the Torah treats rest as owed to the vulnerable.

check.q: What are the three layers of evidence named in the lesson?
choices: The thesis, the body and the conclusion
The quoted text, its context, and how adherents have read it
The author, the date and the publisher
The claim, the counterclaim and the rebuttal
check.why: Evidence starts with the text, adds genre and setting, and then adds the community's reading of the passage.

check.q: According to the lesson, what does the Mishnah list about the Sabbath?
choices: The seven days of creation
The names of the prophets who kept it
Thirty-nine categories of forbidden work
The prayers said in the Temple
check.why: The Mishnah, compiled about 200 CE, lists thirty-nine categories of work, the melakhot, forbidden on the Sabbath.

check.q: What is a warrant?
choices: The reasoning that explains why the evidence supports the claim
A quotation longer than three lines
A citation of the translation used
A secondary source that agrees with the thesis
check.why: The warrant joins text, context and reading to the claim so the reader does not have to guess how they connect.

lessons.title: Diversity Within a Tradition
lessons.mainIdea: Every tradition speaks with many voices, so a strong paper names the branch or school it means and reports where members disagree.
reading: On a Friday evening in Skokie, two Jewish families sit down to Sabbath dinner. In the first, an Orthodox family, no one will drive, cook or switch on a light until Saturday night, and in the morning they will walk to synagogue. In the second, a Reform family, candles are lit and the blessing is said over wine and bread. The next morning they drive to temple and spend the afternoon together, but they do not follow the full set of Sabbath rules. Both families are keeping the Sabbath, in the ways their movements teach.

Judaism today has several *branches*, organized movements with their own teachers and institutions. Orthodox Judaism holds that Jewish law remains binding in full. Conservative Judaism holds that the law is binding but has developed over time. Reform Judaism treats the law as a guide that each generation and each person may interpret. A paper that says Jews rest on the Sabbath by not switching on lights has described one branch and called it the whole. A paper that says many Orthodox Jews do not switch electrical devices on or off on the Sabbath, while Reform Judaism stresses rest and family, has described the tradition.

The same is true everywhere in the course. Hindu teachers have read the Gita in different ways. Shankara read it as a path of knowledge, Ramanuja as a path of devotion, and Gandhi as a guide to selfless action. Confucian thinkers also disagreed. Mencius held that human nature is good and needs nurturing. Xunzi held that it tends toward selfishness and needs shaping by ritual. These are *schools of thought*, lines of interpretation inside one tradition, and a capstone should name them when they bear on the question.

Disagreement inside a tradition is not a sign that its members are confused or inconsistent. It is what happens when many people, across centuries, take the same texts seriously. Report it the way you report any teaching, with attribution. Write most and many where the evidence supports them, and name who holds the minority view. Do not quietly choose the branch that fits your thesis best and present it as the only one. A reader from that tradition would notice, and so would the rubric.

words.d: an organized movement within a tradition, with its own teachers and institutions, such as Orthodox or Reform Judaism
the branch of Judaism that holds Jewish law to be binding in full, as developed in rabbinic tradition
the branch of Judaism that treats Jewish law as a guide each generation and person may interpret
a line of interpretation within a tradition, such as the followers of Mencius or of Xunzi in Confucianism

look.title: Two Tables, One Sabbath
look.text: Table one: candles lit before sunset, no cooking after, no car in the morning, a long walk to synagogue, the day ending with the Havdalah blessing at nightfall. Table two: candles and blessings over wine and bread, a family dinner, a drive to temple on Saturday morning, an afternoon with no work email. Both families say they are keeping the Sabbath.
look.prompt: Write one sentence for a capstone paper that describes Jewish Sabbath practice accurately, using both tables, a qualifier and the names of the branches.

check.q: How does Conservative Judaism differ from Orthodox Judaism, according to the lesson?
choices: Conservative Judaism does not observe the Sabbath
Conservative Judaism rejects the Torah
Conservative Judaism has no rabbis
Conservative Judaism holds that the law is binding but has developed over time
check.why: Orthodox Judaism holds the law binding in full; Conservative Judaism holds it binding but developing; Reform treats it as a guide.

check.q: Mencius and Xunzi disagreed about what?
choices: Whether human nature is good or tends toward selfishness
Whether the Analects should be written down
Whether the Gita is about knowledge or devotion
Whether the Sabbath overrides saving a life
check.why: Both were Confucian thinkers. Mencius held human nature good; Xunzi held it needs shaping by ritual.

check.q: What does the lesson say about disagreement within a tradition?
choices: It shows that members are confused
It should be left out to keep the thesis simple
It is what happens when many people take the same texts seriously, and should be reported with attribution
It means the tradition has no real teaching
check.why: The lesson treats internal disagreement as normal and asks for attribution, qualifiers and names of the schools.

lessons.title: Comparing Without Ranking
lessons.mainIdea: Comparison sets traditions side by side to show where they agree and differ; ranking judges which is best, and the capstone does only the first.
reading: Maya builds a table before she writes her comparison section. Across the top are her three traditions. Down the side are four rows: who is owed rest, who owes it, how often, and why. In the Torah column she writes: the whole household; the head of the household; every seventh day; God's command and the memory of Egypt. In the Gita column: the self; the self; daily, in balance; discipline that ends sorrow. In the Analects column: the people; the ruler; by the seasons; a ruler's virtue. The table makes the pattern visible at a glance.

A *comparison* shows likeness and difference. A *parallel* is a point where two traditions answer in a similar way: both the Torah and the Analects place a duty on someone with power over others. A *contrast* is a point where they differ: the Torah sets a fixed day, while the Analects speak of fitting seasons. Good comparison names both, and then asks why. Here, one answer is that the Torah's command comes as law to a whole people, while the Analects offer advice to rulers.

*Ranking* is different. It judges which tradition is better, truer, wiser or more advanced. The capstone does not rank, for two reasons. No text can settle which tradition is right, so a ranking would rest on opinion, not evidence. And a public school studies religion without favoring or opposing any faith. Watch for ranking words: better, higher, more rational, primitive, superstitious. Watch too for hidden ranking, which uses one tradition as the measuring stick. To say the Analects lack a Sabbath is to measure Confucianism by Judaism.

The opposite mistake is just as unfair. To say all three traditions really teach the same thing about rest is not generous. It erases the differences their adherents care about. A Jew who keeps the Sabbath and a Hindu who practices yoga are not doing the same thing, and neither would want the difference hidden. Fair comparison keeps each tradition's answer in its own terms. It then shows exactly where the answers meet and where they part.

words.d: setting two or more traditions side by side to show where they agree and where they differ
a point where two traditions answer a question in a similar way
a point where two traditions answer a question differently
judging which tradition is better or truer, which the academic study of religion does not do

look.title: Two Comparison Sentences
look.text: Sentence A: Unlike Judaism, Confucianism never developed a proper day of rest, so its view of work is less humane. Sentence B: The Torah sets a fixed weekly day of rest for the whole household, while the Analects ask a ruler to call on the people's labor only at fitting seasons; both place a duty on those with power over others.
look.prompt: Find the ranking and the hidden measuring stick in Sentence A. Then name the parallel and the contrast in Sentence B.

check.q: In Maya's table, what is one parallel between the Torah and the Analects?
choices: Both set a fixed weekly day of rest
Both place the duty on the self alone
Both describe rest as a way to end sorrow
Both place a duty on someone with power over others
check.why: The head of the household in the Torah and the ruler in the Analects each owe rest to those under them.

check.q: Why does the phrase the Analects lack a Sabbath count as hidden ranking?
choices: It measures Confucianism by Judaism's standard
It misquotes the Analects
It uses a word that is not in the Analects
It ranks the Analects above the Torah
check.why: Hidden ranking uses one tradition as the measuring stick. Better: say where the Analects place the duty, in their own terms.

check.q: Why is saying all three traditions teach the same thing about rest a problem?
choices: Because it ranks them
Because it erases differences their adherents care about
Because it quotes too many texts
Because the rubric forbids the word same
check.why: Fair comparison keeps each answer in its own terms; flattening them into sameness misrepresents all three.

lessons.title: Respectful Language
lessons.mainIdea: Use each tradition's own names and terms, attribute every belief, and replace loaded words with accurate, neutral ones.
reading: Compare two sentences. God commanded the Israelites to rest on the seventh day. In the Torah, God commands the Israelites to rest on the seventh day. The first states a religious claim as fact. The second reports what a text says. In a public-school paper the second is correct every time, whatever the writer personally believes. *Attribution*, naming whose belief or text a statement comes from, is the most important habit of respectful language, and it costs only a few words: Muslims hold, according to the Gita, in Sikh teaching.

Use the names traditions use for themselves. Older English books sometimes called Muslims Mohammedans, a term Muslims reject because it suggests they worship Muhammad. The Hebrew Bible is called the *Tanakh* in Jewish tradition and the Old Testament in Christian tradition. Choose the term that fits your sentence, and know why the names differ. Sikhs regard the Guru Granth Sahib as their living Guru, so the name is always given in full. Many academic writers use BCE and CE for dates because the labels do not assume any faith.

Some words carry a judgment inside them. A *loaded word* sounds descriptive but ranks or mocks. Cult, when used for a small or new religious group, implies it is dangerous or false. Myth, when used to mean a false story, dismisses a sacred narrative. Primitive calls an oral tradition backward. Idol worship describes Hindu practice from outside and with scorn. A *murti* is a sacred image in which many Hindus understand the deity to be present. Use that word, with its gloss, instead.

Respect does not mean praise or silence. You may describe hard texts, conflicts and disagreements, including your own reservations if the assignment invites them, as long as you describe them accurately and attribute them. Respect means that a thoughtful member of the tradition could read your sentence and say: yes, that is what we hold, and that is how we would put it. That is the test. Read your draft once more with a member of each tradition in mind before you turn it in.

words.d: naming whose belief or text a statement comes from, as in according to the Qur'an or many Buddhists hold
the Jewish name for the Hebrew Bible, formed from the first letters of its three parts: Torah, Prophets and Writings
a word that sounds descriptive but carries a judgment, such as primitive or cult
in Hindu practice, a sacred image in which many Hindus understand the deity to be present

look.title: Revise the Sentence
look.text: Draft: The Hindus worship idols in their temples, while the Sikhs follow their holy book. Problems to find: a loaded word, a missing term from the tradition itself, and a flat description of the Guru Granth Sahib that leaves out how Sikhs themselves regard it. Each can be fixed in a few words.
look.prompt: Rewrite the draft so that a thoughtful Hindu and a thoughtful Sikh would each recognize their own practice in it.

check.q: Which sentence uses attribution correctly?
choices: God commanded the Israelites to rest
Everyone knows God commanded rest
In the Torah, God commands the Israelites to rest
Rest was commanded by the true God
check.why: It reports what a text says rather than stating a religious claim as fact, which is the rule in a public-school paper.

check.q: Why do Muslims reject the old term Mohammedan?
choices: It suggests they worship Muhammad
It refers only to Shia Muslims
It is an Arabic word for unbeliever
It was used only in the Qur'an
check.why: Muslims worship God alone and regard Muhammad as a prophet, so a name built on his suggests something they reject.

check.q: What is the lesson's test for respectful language?
choices: The sentence praises every tradition
The sentence avoids any mention of disagreement
The sentence uses the longest term available
A thoughtful member of the tradition would recognize the description as accurate
check.why: Respect does not mean praise or silence; it means accurate, attributed description that adherents would recognize.

lessons.title: Handling Difficult Texts
lessons.mainIdea: When a text speaks of war, punishment or unequal roles, quote it accurately, give its context, and report how adherents have read it, without attacking or excusing.
reading: Every scripture in this course contains passages that trouble some readers. The Gita is spoken on a battlefield, where Krishna urges Arjuna to fight. The Hebrew Bible contains laws of war. The Qur'an contains verses about fighting. Early Christian letters give instructions about slaves and wives that many readers today find hard. A capstone question about war, family or forgiveness will lead you to such passages. The worst choices are to skip them, which misrepresents the text, or to use them as weapons, which misrepresents the tradition.

Treat a difficult text exactly like any other: text, context, reading. Take Qur'an 2:190, which tells believers to fight those who fight them but not to overstep limits. The *historical context*, as Muslim tradition presents it, is the conflict between the early Muslim community at Medina and its opponents from Mecca. Many Muslim scholars have read the verse as permitting fighting in defense and within limits. Interpretations have varied across fourteen centuries and among legal schools. Your paper can say all of that in four sentences, each attributed.

Readings of the Gita show how much interpretation matters. Some Hindu commentators read the battle as real and teach that a warrior's duty, his *dharma*, required him to fight. Gandhi, who practiced nonviolence, read the battlefield as an *allegory*, a story in which the fighting stands for the inner struggle between right and wrong. Both readings come from within the tradition. A paper on war that quotes Krishna's command without these readings has told half the story.

Two cautions keep a paper fair. Do not apologize for a tradition by hiding a hard verse, and do not prosecute it by quoting that verse alone. Also keep the text separate from the history. What a scripture says and what some members did in its name are different questions, and each needs its own evidence and dates. Describe violence, persecution and conflict factually, with places and dates, and let the reader weigh them.

words.d: the time, place and events surrounding a text, as the tradition and historians describe them
a story in which characters and events stand for ideas, such as a battle standing for an inner struggle
in Hindu tradition, duty and the right way to live, which differs with a person's role and stage of life

look.title: Fighting and Its Limits
look.text: The Qur'an tells believers to fight, in the way of God, those who fight against them, but not to go beyond the limits, because God does not love those who overstep them.
look.cite: Qur'an 2:190, paraphrased from the standard text
look.prompt: Write the context and reading layers for this verse in two attributed sentences, using the lesson's information.

check.q: According to the lesson, what are the two worst ways to handle a difficult text?
choices: Quoting it and citing it
Skipping it, or using it alone as a weapon
Giving its context and its reading
Naming its genre and its translator
check.why: Skipping a hard text misrepresents the scripture; quoting it alone as a weapon misrepresents the tradition.

check.q: How did Gandhi read the battlefield of the Gita?
choices: As a record of a battle he wanted repeated
As a law for all soldiers
As an allegory of the inner struggle between right and wrong
As a later addition to be ignored
check.why: Gandhi, who practiced nonviolence, read the battle as an allegory, while other Hindu commentators read it as a warrior's real duty.

check.q: Why does the lesson say to keep the text separate from the history?
choices: Because history is not part of the study of religion
Because texts have no dates
Because the rubric counts only texts
Because what a scripture says and what some members did in its name are different questions needing their own evidence
check.why: Each question needs its own evidence and dates; merging them misrepresents both the text and the people.

lessons.title: Building the Written Essay
lessons.mainIdea: The essay moves from the question to the thesis, gives each tradition its own section of layered evidence, then compares them and names the limits of the study.
reading: The written essay has five parts, in order. The *introduction* poses the question, explains in a sentence or two why it matters, and ends with the thesis. Next come three body sections, one for each tradition. Each section follows the five moves from earlier in this chapter: claim, text, context, reading and warrant. Then comes a comparison section that sets the three answers side by side. The conclusion states the answer again in fresh words and names what the study could not settle. Last is a works-cited list with full information for every translation and secondary source.

There are two ways to organize a comparison. In *block structure*, you finish one tradition before starting the next, then compare at the end. It is easier to write, and it keeps each tradition's answer whole. In *point-by-point structure*, each section takes one row of the comparison table, such as who is owed rest, and answers it for all three traditions at once. It makes the comparison sharper but can break up each tradition's voice. Many strong capstones use block structure for the body and point-by-point structure for the comparison section.

The comparison section is where the thesis is proved, and it is the part students most often rush. Walk the reader through each parallel and each contrast. Then give your best explanation for the pattern, grounded in genre and context. Maya might explain that the Torah speaks as law to a people, the Gita as teaching to one person, and the Analects as advice to rulers. So each locates the duty of rest where its own genre points: the community, the self or the state.

The conclusion should name the study's *limits*. Maya read the Gita in English, not Sanskrit. She used three passages from traditions with thousands of pages. She interviewed one family from one branch of Judaism. Naming limits does not weaken a paper. It tells the reader exactly how far the evidence reaches, and that is a mark of honest scholarship. End with the question the study opened but could not answer. For Maya, it is how each tradition would speak to a modern worker's schedule.

words.d: the opening of an essay, which poses the question, explains why it matters and ends with the thesis
an essay organization that discusses one tradition completely before moving to the next
an essay organization that answers one part of the question for all traditions before moving to the next part
the boundaries of what a study's evidence can show, such as reading in translation or using a few passages

look.title: A Word Budget for the Capstone Essay
look.cite: Suggested plan for a capstone essay of about 2,300 words, following Maya's three traditions
look.prompt: The comparison section gets the largest share. Using the lesson, explain why, and say what would go wrong if it got only 100 words.

check.q: What does the introduction of the capstone essay end with?
choices: The thesis
The works-cited list
The longest quotation
The limits of the study
check.why: The introduction poses the question, explains why it matters, and ends with the thesis the essay will prove.

check.q: What is point-by-point structure?
choices: Finishing one tradition before starting the next
Quoting one verse per paragraph
Answering one part of the question for all traditions before moving to the next part
Listing every point in the introduction
check.why: Point-by-point structure takes one row of the comparison table at a time, which sharpens the comparison.

check.q: Why does the lesson say naming limits does not weaken a paper?
choices: Because teachers do not read the conclusion
Because it tells the reader exactly how far the evidence reaches
Because limits replace the need for a thesis
Because every paper has the same limits
check.why: Stating that the Gita was read in English, or that few passages were used, is a mark of honest scholarship.

lessons.title: The Oral Presentation
lessons.mainIdea: A strong presentation states the thesis early, reads one key text per tradition accurately with its citation, and treats sacred words and objects with care.
reading: A listener cannot flip back a page. That one fact shapes every choice in an *oral presentation*. State the question and thesis in the first minute and show the thesis on screen. Use *signposts*, spoken markers that tell listeners where they are, such as: that was the Torah's answer; now the Gita's. Give each tradition one key passage, not five. Put the quotation on a slide with the citation and translation beneath it. Then read it aloud slowly, exactly as printed.

Reading a sacred text aloud is a responsibility. Practice every name and term until you can say it without stumbling: Bhagavad Gita, Analects, Guru Granth Sahib, Tanakh. If you are unsure of a pronunciation, ask your teacher or a member of the tradition, not a guess from spelling. Say the translation aloud as well: in the King James translation, or in a paraphrase of chapter 6 of the Gita. Your listeners should always know whose words they are hearing.

Visual aids help when they carry information. A photograph of a Sabbath table, a map of where the Analects were compiled, or a comparison table can all teach. Some images need care. Many Muslims avoid any picture of the Prophet Muhammad, so a presentation should not show one. Physical scriptures also need care. Sikhs keep the Guru Granth Sahib covered on a raised platform, and many Muslims handle a copy of the Qur'an only in a state of ritual cleanliness. A printed excerpt is usually the respectful choice for a classroom.

Do not perform another tradition's ritual or wear its religious clothing as a costume. You may describe a ritual, show a respectful photograph, or play a recording made and shared by the community. The line is between showing how adherents practice and imitating it for effect. Close the presentation by returning to the thesis in one sentence. Then invite questions, which the next lesson takes up.

words.d: a spoken report to an audience, usually supported by slides or other visual aids
a spoken marker that tells listeners where they are in a presentation, such as now the second tradition
an image, table or object shown to an audience to carry information during a presentation

look.title: Maya's Nine-Minute Plan
look.cite: Sample timing for a nine-minute capstone presentation, with questions to follow
look.prompt: Maya spends one minute on her question and thesis. What must she say in that minute so that the rest of the presentation makes sense to a listener?

check.q: What is a signpost in an oral presentation?
choices: A slide with a quotation on it
The final sentence of the thesis
A citation shown under a quotation
A spoken marker telling listeners where they are in the talk
check.why: Listeners cannot flip back, so signposts such as that was the Torah's answer; now the Gita's keep them oriented.

check.q: Why does the lesson advise against showing a picture of the Prophet Muhammad?
choices: Because many Muslims avoid any picture of him
Because no pictures of Arabia exist
Because the Qur'an forbids all images of people
Because the image would be too small to see
check.why: Many Muslims avoid images of the Prophet, and a respectful presentation honors that practice.

check.q: Which choice follows the lesson's guidance on rituals?
choices: Wearing a tradition's religious clothing to set the mood
Leading the class in another tradition's prayer
Showing a respectful photograph of a practice and describing it
Acting out a ceremony for effect
check.why: The line is between showing how adherents practice and imitating it; describing and showing respectfully is on the right side.

lessons.title: Answering Questions
lessons.mainIdea: Answer audience questions by returning to the texts, naming diversity within the tradition, and saying plainly when you do not know.
reading: Questions after a presentation come in four kinds. A *clarifying question* asks you to explain something again: what does moderate mean in the Gita passage? A challenge tests your claim: isn't the Gita really about war, not rest? A personal question asks what you believe. A correction comes from someone who knows the tradition, perhaps a member of it, who says you have something wrong. Each deserves a different answer, and none should make you defensive.

For clarifying questions and challenges, go back to the evidence. Restate the question briefly so everyone hears it. Then answer from the text, its context or how adherents read it. When a classmate asked Maya whether the Gita was about war, she agreed that it is set on a battlefield. She then explained that chapter 6 teaches balance as part of Arjuna's larger instruction, and that commentators read the setting in different ways. A *concession*, granting the part of a challenge that is true, makes the rest of an answer more believable.

Personal questions have a simple answer. The assignment asked what each tradition would say, not what you believe. You may choose to share your own view if your teacher allows it. You may also decline politely, as Maya did, and point back to the evidence. Either choice is fine. Do not let a personal answer slip into ranking. You would not want a classmate's faith, or lack of one, judged by your presentation.

A correction is a gift, even when it stings. Thank the person. If they are a member of the tradition, report what they said as how they, or their community, understand it: that is a helpful reading, and I will check it against my sources. Then check it. Sometimes the correction is right, and your paper improves. Sometimes it reflects one branch among many, and your paper can mention it. When you do not know the answer, say so: I did not find that in my sources.

words.d: a question that asks a presenter to explain or restate something more clearly
granting the part of a challenge or objection that is true before answering the rest
a statement from a listener that something in the presentation is inaccurate, to be thanked for and checked

look.title: The Ruler and the Seasons
look.text: Confucius said that to govern a state of a thousand chariots, a ruler must attend to affairs with reverence and keep faith with the people, spend with restraint and care for others, and call on the people's labor only at the proper seasons.
look.prompt: A classmate asks: this is about farming seasons, so how is it about rest? Write a two-sentence answer that begins with a concession and then returns to the text.

check.q: Isn't the Gita really about war? is an example of which kind of question?
choices: A personal question
A challenge
A correction
A clarifying question
check.why: It tests the presenter's claim that the Gita speaks about rest, so it is a challenge to be answered from the evidence.

check.q: What is a concession?
choices: Refusing to answer a question
Changing the thesis during the presentation
Granting the part of a challenge that is true before answering the rest
Asking the audience to vote
check.why: Maya conceded the Gita is set on a battlefield, then showed that chapter 6 teaches balance, which made her answer more believable.

check.q: How does the lesson suggest responding when a member of a tradition corrects you?
choices: Argue until the audience agrees with you
Ignore it, since the paper is finished
Replace your whole thesis immediately
Thank the person, report it as their community's understanding, and check it against sources
check.why: A correction may improve the paper or reflect one branch among many; either way it is thanked, attributed and checked.

lessons.title: Reading the Rubric
lessons.mainIdea: The rubric weights evidence most heavily, and it rewards fairness, attribution and diversity within traditions as much as it rewards organization.
reading: A *rubric* is a scoring guide that lists what a piece of work will be judged on and describes each level of quality. The capstone rubric has six *criteria*, or standards: thesis, evidence and context, diversity and fairness, organization, citation, and delivery. Each has a number of points. Reading the rubric before you write is not gaming the assignment. It is reading the assignment carefully, the same way you read a sacred text with author, audience and purpose in mind.

The weights tell you what matters most. Evidence and context carry the most points because the whole project rests on them. A paper with a brilliant thesis and thin evidence has asserted, not argued. Diversity and fairness come second. That criterion asks whether you named branches and schools, and used qualifiers. It also asks whether you attributed every belief and avoided loaded words. Many students lose points here not through disrespect but through the small word all.

Each criterion has *performance levels*, often four: exceeds, meets, approaching and beginning. The descriptions make the difference concrete. For evidence, meets might read: quotes a primary text for each tradition, with context. Exceeds might read: quotes a primary text for each tradition, gives its context and reports how adherents have read it, including a disagreement within the tradition. The gap between the two is the third layer of evidence from earlier in this chapter.

Use the rubric twice. Before drafting, turn each criterion into a question for your notes: do I have a primary text for each tradition? a branch named for each? After drafting, score yourself honestly on each line. Then revise the lowest line first. A paper that moves from approaching to meets on evidence gains more than one that polishes its introduction. The rubric is a map of where your next hour of work will do the most good.

words.d: a scoring guide that lists the criteria for a piece of work and describes each level of quality
one standard on which work is judged, such as thesis or citation; the plural is criteria
one step on a rubric's scale, such as exceeds, meets, approaching or beginning

look.title: The Capstone Rubric's Weights
look.cite: Sample capstone rubric used in this course
look.prompt: Evidence and fairness together make up half the points. Which two lessons in this chapter would help most with those criteria, and why?

check.q: Which criterion carries the most points on the capstone rubric?
choices: Evidence and context
Thesis
Delivery
Citation
check.why: Evidence and context carry 30 of 100 points, because the whole project rests on quoted, explained, well-read texts.

check.q: According to the lesson, what often separates meets from exceeds on the evidence criterion?
choices: Using more slides
Quoting longer passages
Writing a longer introduction
Reporting how adherents have read the text, including a disagreement within the tradition
check.why: The gap is the third layer of evidence: how the community reads the passage, with its internal diversity.

check.q: After drafting, which line of the rubric does the lesson say to revise first?
choices: The line with the most points
The line where you scored lowest
The introduction
The delivery line
check.why: The rubric is a map of where the next hour of work does the most good, so the weakest criterion comes first.

lessons.title: Peer Review Against the Rubric
lessons.mainIdea: A peer reviewer checks a partner's draft line by line against the rubric and the texts, and gives specific, kind, usable comments.
reading: Before the final draft, the class trades papers. *Peer review* is the practice of having a classmate read and comment on a draft before it is graded. Scholars do it before their work is published, and it catches what a writer cannot see in their own pages. Your partner has read the same course and knows the same terms. That makes them the right reader to ask whether your evidence holds and your language is fair.

A good reviewer works through the rubric one criterion at a time rather than reading once and saying it was good. Underline the thesis. Is there a clause for each tradition? For each body section, find the claim, the text, the context, the reading and the warrant, and mark any missing one. Circle every all, every, never and always, and ask whether the evidence supports it. Check two citations by opening the text to the verse cited. Mark any sentence that states a belief without attribution.

Comments should be *specific*, kind and usable. Good job teaches nothing. This paragraph on the Analects has a quotation but no context helps. So does: you say all Hindus practice yoga, but your source is about one teacher's reading of chapter 6. Frame suggestions as questions when you can: could you name which branch of Judaism this family belongs to? A reviewer is not grading. The goal is a stronger paper.

Receiving comments takes practice too. Read them all before responding. Sort them into the ones you agree with, the ones you need to check, and the ones you will set aside, with a reason for each. When a reviewer and your sources disagree, the sources win. Then revise. Many teachers ask for a short note with the final draft listing the three most important changes you made and why. Writing it shows you how much the paper grew.

words.d: having a classmate or fellow scholar read and comment on a draft before it is graded or published
pointing to an exact sentence, paragraph or source, rather than giving general praise or blame
rewriting a draft to improve its argument, evidence or language, not only its spelling

look.title: Three Comments on One Paragraph
look.text: Comment A: Nice paragraph! Comment B: You quote Exodus 20:8-10 and give its context, but I did not see how Jewish tradition reads it today. Could you add one sentence on a branch? Comment C: Your paragraph says Jews cannot use electricity on the Sabbath; is that true of all Jews, or of many Orthodox Jews?
look.prompt: Rank these comments by how useful they are to the writer, and explain which rubric criterion each of the useful ones connects to.

check.q: According to the lesson, how should a reviewer read a partner's draft?
choices: Once, then give an overall grade
Only for spelling and punctuation
Criterion by criterion, marking missing layers of evidence and unsupported words like all
Only the introduction and conclusion
check.why: A good reviewer works through the rubric one line at a time and checks claims, evidence, qualifiers and citations.

check.q: Which comment is the most specific and usable?
choices: This paragraph on the Analects has a quotation but no context
Good job
I liked it
Needs more work
check.why: It points to an exact paragraph and names the missing layer of evidence, so the writer knows what to fix.

check.q: What does the lesson say to do when a reviewer's comment and your sources disagree?
choices: Follow the reviewer, since they are a fresh reader
Delete the paragraph
Ask the audience to decide
Follow the sources
check.why: Comments are sorted and checked; when a reviewer and the sources disagree, the sources win.

lessons.title: What the Study of Religion Is For
lessons.mainIdea: The academic study of religion helps people in a diverse society read carefully, understand their neighbors and disagree fairly, without asking anyone to believe or disbelieve.
reading: In September 1893, during the World's Columbian Exposition, the World's Parliament of Religions opened in Chicago. It met in a new building on Michigan Avenue that now houses the Art Institute. Speakers from many traditions addressed large audiences. Swami Vivekananda, a Hindu monk from India, began his first speech with the words Sisters and Brothers of America, and the crowd rose to applaud. The Parliament is often called one of the first formal meetings of the world's religions in the West.

Seventy years later, in Abington School District v. Schempp in 1963, the United States Supreme Court ruled that public schools may not lead devotional Bible reading. Justice Tom Clark's opinion added that studying the Bible and religion objectively, as part of a secular education, is consistent with the First Amendment. This course rests on that line. The academic *study of religion* describes what traditions teach and how people live them. It does not ask anyone to accept or reject them. Students of every faith and of none take the same course on equal terms.

What is the study for? Part of the answer is practical. Americans live among a wide variety of religious communities. A recent national survey found about six in ten Americans identify as Christian, nearly three in ten with no religion, and the rest with other traditions. Chicago's neighborhoods hold churches, synagogues, mosques, gurdwaras, temples and the Bahá'í House of Worship in nearby Wilmette. A nurse, a teacher, a store manager or a neighbor will meet all of them. *Religious literacy*, a working knowledge of what traditions teach and practice, makes those meetings better.

Part of the answer is about the skills themselves. You have learned to read a text for its author, audience and purpose, and to quote and cite it exactly. You have learned to report disagreement inside a tradition, to compare without ranking, and to answer a challenge from evidence. Those skills work on a news article, a court opinion or a campaign speech as well as on a psalm. The capstone's last task is a short *reflection*: a paragraph on what you now read differently.

words.d: the academic field that describes what religious traditions teach and how people live them, without judging whether they are true
a working knowledge of what the world's traditions teach and practice, and the ability to discuss them accurately
a gathering of speakers from many traditions held in Chicago in 1893, often called one of the first of its kind in the West
a short piece of writing in which a student considers what they learned and how their thinking changed

look.title: The Court on Studying Religion
look.text: Justice Clark wrote that a person's education may not be complete without a study of comparative religion and its relationship to civilization, and that nothing in the Court's ruling means the Bible cannot be studied for its literary and historic qualities when presented objectively as part of a secular program of education.
look.cite: Abington School District v. Schempp, U.S. Supreme Court, 1963, opinion of Justice Tom C. Clark, paraphrased
look.prompt: What is the difference between the devotional Bible reading the Court ruled out and the study this course has done? Use the word objectively in your answer.

check.q: Where was the 1893 World's Parliament of Religions held?
choices: Wilmette, at the Bahá'í House of Worship
Chicago, in a building on Michigan Avenue that now houses the Art Institute
Washington, D.C., at the Supreme Court
Skokie, at a public library
check.why: The Parliament met in Chicago during the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition, in the building that now houses the Art Institute.

check.q: What did the Supreme Court's 1963 Schempp decision say about public schools and religion?
choices: Schools must teach only one tradition
Schools may not mention religion at all
Schools may not lead devotional Bible reading, but may study religion objectively
Schools must hold a daily prayer
check.why: The Court ruled out devotional Bible reading, while Justice Clark's opinion affirmed objective study as consistent with the First Amendment.

check.q: What is religious literacy?
choices: Belief in every religion at once
The ability to read sacred texts in their original languages
Membership in a religious community
A working knowledge of what traditions teach and practice, and the ability to discuss them accurately
check.why: Religious literacy is knowledge and accurate discussion, not belief or membership, and it serves people in a diverse society.

review.q: Which thesis follows the chapter's model?
choices: The Torah grounds rest in God's command, the Gita in a disciplined self's balance, and the Analects in a ruler's virtue
Judaism, Hinduism and Confucianism all value rest
Judaism has the most humane view of rest
All religions teach the same thing about rest
review.why: It answers for each tradition, names each grounding and compares them; the others list, rank or flatten.

review.q: A paragraph quotes Exodus 20:8-10, explains that it is law given at Sinai, and reports the Mishnah's thirty-nine categories. What is still missing?
choices: A second translation
The warrant that connects the evidence to the claim
A visual aid
A personal opinion
review.why: Text, context and reading are present, but the warrant explains why they support the claim.

review.q: Which sentence reports diversity within Judaism accurately?
choices: Jews never drive on Saturday
Judaism has no rules about the Sabbath
Many Orthodox Jews avoid driving on the Sabbath, while Reform Judaism stresses rest and family
Only rabbis keep the Sabbath
review.why: It names the branches and uses a qualifier, as the lesson on diversity within a tradition asks.

review.q: What is the difference between comparison and ranking?
choices: Comparison uses more traditions than ranking
Ranking is used only in oral presentations
There is no difference
Comparison shows likeness and difference; ranking judges which tradition is better
review.why: The capstone compares but does not rank, because no text can settle which tradition is right.

review.q: Which term is the Jewish name for the Hebrew Bible?
choices: Tanakh
Talmud
Tafsir
Tractate
review.why: Tanakh comes from the first letters of Torah, Prophets and Writings. Tafsir is Islamic commentary; the Talmud is rabbinic discussion.

review.q: How did Gandhi's reading of the Gita differ from readings that take the battle as real?
choices: He rejected the Gita
He read the battle as an allegory of the inner struggle between right and wrong
He read it as a law code for soldiers
He read it as a history of India
review.why: Gandhi, who practiced nonviolence, read the battlefield as allegory; other commentators taught a warrior's duty to fight.

review.q: In a presentation, which is the respectful way to include a practice from another tradition?
choices: Wear its religious clothing as a costume
Lead the class in its prayer
Show a respectful photograph and describe what adherents do
Act out the ceremony for effect
review.why: The line is between showing how adherents practice and imitating it for effect.

review.q: Which choice best states what the academic study of religion is for, according to the chapter?
choices: Deciding which tradition is true
Encouraging students to join a tradition
Encouraging students to leave religion behind
Helping people read carefully, understand neighbors and disagree fairly
review.why: The study describes without asking anyone to believe or disbelieve, and builds religious literacy for a diverse society.
